q1: There is no standard chemotherapy for this tumor, and I would not invent an entity to create one. If systemic treatment is started now, the option I would use is single-agent oral temozolomide. I would discuss, and not start, doxorubicin with or without ifosfamide. I would not use temozolomide plus bevacizumab, lomustine, gemcitabine/docetaxel, or an intensive translocation-defined sarcoma regimen. The 2026-11-04 diagnosis remains high-grade spindle cell/mesenchymal neoplasm, NOS: STAT6 negative, no NAB2::STAT6, entity unestablished. Solitary fibrous tumor is excluded, so the temozolomide-bevacizumab regimen used in that disease does not apply. No FET::CREB, SS18, CIC, BCOR, or DICER1 result is in the record, so Ewing-type, synovial, CIC, or BCOR multiagent therapy is not justified. This is not established glioblastoma, MGMT is unknown, and the completed 60 Gy was focal radiotherapy without concurrent temozolomide, so this would not be Stupp therapy. Temozolomide is the least-bad empiric cytotoxic if one is started: it enters the CNS, is tolerable at ECOG 1 in a 34-year-old, can be stopped if a confirmed target or a real entity appears, and does not commit him to anthracycline cardiotoxicity or ifosfamide encephalopathy. Doxorubicin-based treatment is the standard cytotoxic approach only for confirmed advanced soft-tissue sarcoma; doxorubicin has negligible CNS penetration, ifosfamide neurotoxicity is a poor trade after brain irradiation, and that toxicity is not warranted while the entity is unknown and the plasma assay drawn 2026-12-15 is due on this visit. Gemcitabine/docetaxel, trabectedin, and pazopanib are later-line or histology-selected and are not appropriate empiric intracranial therapy. The growth MRI is 2026-12-12, seven days after radiotherapy, and the observation compares it with the 2026-10-17 pre-resection baseline, so it is not clean proof of progression. No new deficit is documented. If he remains clinically stable I would obtain a current brain and spine MRI and wait days for the result already due, rather than start cytotoxic therapy today. The stable unbiopsied C6 nodule is not proven dissemination and is not itself an indication for chemotherapy. Body CT or PET was never documented and should still be done so an extracranial primary is not missed, but it does not create a regimen. Blood counts and organ function are not in the record and are required before any dose, as is fertility counseling. This is not a treatment order.
q2: No. I would not add a second chemotherapy drug. Several weeks of single-agent oral temozolomide without significant toxicity is the expected course of this drug, not evidence of under-treatment and not a reason to intensify. No response MRI is described, and this interval is too short to call benefit or failure. No combination has a rationale in high-grade spindle cell/mesenchymal neoplasm, NOS. Adding lomustine would copy a strategy limited to MGMT-methylated glioblastoma, which this is not, and MGMT is not reported. Adding bevacizumab would copy solitary fibrous tumor practice, which STAT6-negative, NAB2::STAT6-negative histology has excluded. Adding doxorubicin, ifosfamide, a platinum, or irinotecan would import a sarcoma or embryonal regimen without a defining diagnosis and would add marrow, cardiac, bladder, or neurologic toxicity while the entity is still unestablished. A second drug would also make response and toxicity impossible to attribute and would spend marrow reserve that may be needed if a later tissue-confirmed target, trial, or real sarcoma regimen appears. Continue single-agent temozolomide and judge it on a planned brain and spine MRI. If that MRI shows progression, the next step is a change of strategy, with sarcoma oncology if the entity is still NOS, not stacking a second empiric cytotoxic onto temozolomide. Revisit a combination only if a later integrated diagnosis makes that combination specific to the entity.
q3: No. I will not stop temozolomide and I will not change to targeted therapy. This is a peripheral-blood ctDNA report, the least reliable sample for a CNS-restricted tumor, and it does not prove that the intracranial neoplasm carries these alterations. They were not established on the resection, the prior tumor panel was limited, and a plasma call is not tissue confirmation. The four-alteration pattern is also not a credible single-tumor genotype and must not be used to name the entity. An FGFR2 fusion and a KRAS alteration are alternative MAPK drivers and are ordinarily mutually exclusive; co-reporting them, plus STK11, which with KRAS is a lung-adenocarcinoma pattern, and CTNNB1, a driver in unrelated tumors, suggests artifact, non-tumor DNA, low-confidence calls, or an unrelated clone rather than an FGFR-driven CNS mesenchymal tumor. Even if the fusion were real and tumor-derived, concurrent KRAS is a resistance mechanism to FGFR inhibition and argues against pemigatinib, futibatinib, or erdafitinib. Those drugs have no indication for an unconfirmed CNS mesenchymal neoplasm on plasma DNA, and their CNS activity is not established. The KRAS allele is not specified, so this is not a G12C decision, and a plasma KRAS call would still not justify stopping chemotherapy here. STK11 and CTNNB1 have no approved agent that should replace chemotherapy in this disease. MSI and TMB are not reported, so there is no tumor-agnostic immunotherapy trigger. He is tolerating temozolomide; stopping it would trade that for inhibitor toxicity without evidence the brain tumor is the source. Continue temozolomide. Obtain variant allele fractions, fusion partner, read support, and clonal-hematopoiesis or germline annotation from the laboratory. Confirm any fusion on the 2026-10-28 tumor tissue before a targeted agent is even discussed; repeat brain biopsy only if that tissue is exhausted and neurosurgery judges it safe. Do not biopsy the 5 mm C6 nodule for this. Molecular tumor board review is appropriate. Do not start an FGFR, KRAS, WNT, or other targeted agent on this report, and do not declare a final histologic entity from it.
